body.text: Today, a girl in Afghanistan cannot go to school past the sixth grade. Her older sister cannot enter a university, a park, or a beauty salon. Her mother cannot travel far without a male relative, cannot hold most jobs, and under a 2024 Taliban law, even her voice is not to be heard in public. The United Nations counts 2.4 million Afghan girls shut out of school, and its experts call the system a gender apartheid.

None of this is new. Twenty-six years ago, the Taliban ran most of the country, and the rules for girls and women were nearly identical: no school, no work, no leaving home without a mahram (a male chaperone), the chadari (an Afghan burqa), a beating in the street for a woman who showed an ankle. The world mostly looked away.
Less remembered is what Afghan women did about it.

In June 2000, the year before the September 11 attacks, about 300 Afghan women gathered in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, and wrote down their own bill of rights. They called it the Declaration of the Essential Rights of Afghan Women. It is one of the most important documents in Afghanistan’s modern history, and almost nobody has read it.
I spoke at length with Nasrine Gross, the Afghan-American writer who helped draft the declaration and read it aloud to that hall in Dushanbe 26 years ago.

The conference was organized by NEGAR-Support of Women of Afghanistan, a small Paris-based group led by Shoukria Haidar, an Afghan exile living in France. Women came from inside Afghanistan, from the refugee camps in Pakistan, Iran, and Tajikistan, and from the diaspora in Europe and the United States; most of the 300 women in attendance were refugees.

Gross and Haidar worked from a preliminary draft prepared by NEGAR, incorporating advice Gross had received from her mother before leaving for Dushanbe. Her mother was Roqia Abubakr, one of the first four women elected to the First House of the People, the lower chamber of Afghanistan’s parliament, in 1965. She had also served on the revision commission for Afghanistan’s 1964 constitution.
“She told me, ‘Do this, don’t do that,’” Gross told me, laughing.
The women of Afghanistan who gathered in Dushanbe in 2000 were not inventing rights from nothing. They were seeking to get back what their mothers had already achieved.

A committee took the draft on the first day, worked through the night, and read it to the full assembly on the second morning. Gross was the designated reader. She told me she was shaking, afraid the women would object to the declaration. When she finished, she kept her eyes on the paper. Then one woman stood up, in tears, clapping. Then the whole room was on its feet.
“That was the vote,” Gross said.

Then they did something clever. The assembly declared the text closed: Afghan women had written it, and no man, government, or foreign organization could edit it. What outsiders could do was sign a separate statement of support. The world could only endorse it.

The declaration is short and does not mince words. Its first section says the Taliban’s rules on women stand in total opposition to international law, that women and their children live in permanent danger, and that poverty and the ban on movement push women into prostitution, forced marriage, and the trafficking of their daughters. Read in 2026, every line still accurate describes Afghanistan.

The second section cites the U.N. Charter, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), the Beijing Declaration, and, pointedly, the Afghan Constitutions of 1964 and 1977.
“We were grounding our claim in Afghanistan’s own legal history; we were not importing it from anywhere else,” Gross told me.

Then come the ten rights: equality between men and women; personal safety and freedom from torture; physical and mental health for women and their children; equal protection under the law; education in all intellectual and physical disciplines; fair conditions of work; freedom of movement; freedom of thought, speech, assembly and political participation; the right to take part in culture, with theater, music and sports specifically named.
Listed ninth was the right to wear, or not to wear, the chadari covering the full body, including the face, or the scarf.

In 2000, and even more so in late 2001, Western conversation about Afghan women was all about the burqa, a garment worn by women in parts of the Muslim world that covers their entire body and face in public. It’s known as the chadari in Afghanistan. Even now, in 2026, female U.N. officials dealing with Taliban leaders concede to doing so fully covered and wearing long scarves, in the hope of persuading them to respect Afghan women’s rights. Treating those rights as a favor to be won from the very men who deny them makes a mockery of the very effort.

Twenty-six years ago, Afghan women gathered in Dushanbe and put into writing the rights they claimed for themselves. When it came to the chadari, they refused to make the garment itself the issue. They did not demand its abolition; they demanded that every woman be free to decide for herself whether to wear it.
The closing section of the declaration proclaimed that these rights were ones Afghan women own for themselves, and the text a draft they will keep amending. It was written to go into a constitution.

Not long after the gathering in Dushanbe, five or six of the women crossed into the Panjshir Valley to see Ahmad Shah Massoud, “Amer Sahib,” as Gross still calls him, meaning the commander. He was fighting the Taliban from the last unconquered corner of the country. There is a photograph of Massoud seated among the women on a sofa, the declaration in his hand, a pen in hand as he signs.

Massoud was not a man who acted on impulse, Gross told me. He read the delcaration. Above his signature, he wrote one line: that he supported it with consideration for the national and religious values of Afghanistan. His enemy, the Taliban, had erased women from public life and called it Islam. The world, meanwhile, suspected the mujahideen of the Northern Alliance of which Massoud was a part would be no better once in power. Massoud’s signature flew in the face of those suspicions. Gross said it changed how the resistance could talk to foreigners: the commander could now raise women’s rights openly, pointing to a document written by Afghan women, not Western donors. A month after Massoud’s September 10, 2021 assassination by al-Qaida, Nasrine Gross told CNN Massoud had been one of Afghan women’s best friends.

Gross also recalls going to Burhanuddin Rabbani, then Afghanistan’s president despite the Taliban’s almost complete control of the country at the time, after she had secured Massoud’s signature, to sign. Gross said he declined to give his support, citing Taliban pressure. He signed only in December 2001, the day he peacefully handed power to Hamid Karzai.

In the year after that meeting in Dushanbe, Haidar collected several hundred thousand signatures from refugee communities across Europe; Gross worked in the United States with no funding, no office, and no car. Betty Friedan, a leading American feminist, signed. So did the president of the European Parliament and the Belgian Senate.

On September 9, 2001, Gross was in Khwaja Bahauddin, in northern Afghanistan, with a group of American women. She was in the house next door when two al-Qaida men posing as journalists assassinated Massoud. She went to Panjshir for the funeral, one of four or five women among thousands of men. That, she told me, was the day she decided to give the rest of her life to Afghanistan. She went to the most remote parts of the country, collecting signatures from soldiers, widows, and schoolgirls.

During an October 2001 interview with CNN, after spending weeks traversing Afghanistan, Gross said that the Taliban were the first government in history to revoke, by written decree, all the rights of half a country’s citizens. She brought her navy blue chadari to demonstrate. Pulling it on over her head live on air, said said, “Look at me: I have become invisible.”
That November the Washington Post profiled her under the headline “Thinking Outside the Burqa.”

By 2003 the collected signatures weighed several hundred pounds. Gross and Haidar had carried 80 pounds of them to Kabul a few pounds at a time on their trips, because air freight was too expensive. In July that year NEGAR presented the signatures to the Revision Commission of the Constitution, hundreds of thousands of names, with one demand: equal citizenship for women and men in the new constitution.
Hamid Karzai, the interim president of Afghanistan in 2002, affirmed its support by signing the declaration.

Then came the part Gross is proudest of. In a corridor at the commission offices, she met one of its women members in the revision commission, a former children’s judge. They had read the declaration, the judge said, and wanted equality in the text, but feared wording that would inflame people still shaped by Taliban thinking. Gross gave her the words to move forward: keep it short, equal rights for all citizens, women and men. Article 22 of the 2004 constitution ends: “The citizens of Afghanistan, man and woman, have equal rights and duties before the law.” That, according to Gross, is mostly her sentence.

Nobody thanked them. When the money and the NGOs arrived after 2001, Gross said, no one mentioned that Afghan women had done the hard work first, alone and unfunded, while the Taliban still held Kabul.

And now that Afghan Constitution is gone; the Taliban discarded it in 2021. But the Dushanbe Declaration never belonged to a state. It belonged to the women who wrote it. Read its ten rights today and you will find a list of what the Taliban have taken, in the words of the women whose rights have been repeatedly violated. Women inside Afghanistan are still fighting to reclaim those rights.

Years ago, Nasrin Gross, Shukria Haidar, and the 300 women who gathered in Dushanbe helped keep the voice of Afghan women alive. Today, many more Afghan women are carrying that struggle forward around the world. Through the End Gender Apartheid campaign, they are once again naming the injustice themselves and calling on the world to act.

Before U.N. officials next sit down with Taliban leaders, they should read the declaration Afghan women adopted in Dushanbe 26 years ago. And if they say those meetings are meant to protect Afghan women’s rights, they should first listen to the women leading that fight today and let their demands shape what is discussed at the table.
